overview: White develops with 2.Nc3 instead of the fianchetto and often follows 2...Nf6 with 3.Bg5, hitting the f6 knight and preparing e4. Black answers ...d5 (when Bxf6 exf6 gives doubled f-pawns but the bishop pair) or ...e6 and ...Be7. White tries e4 with a lead in development; Black can reach a Stonewall or Classical set-up.

white_ideas.idea: Pin with Bg5, Bxf6 and play e4 or e3 and Bd3 for development and central play.
Keep options of e4 breaks and Nf3 without committing to the fianchetto.

black_ideas.idea: Play ...d5 and ...e6 or ...c6 with a Stonewall-type set-up.
Accept doubled f-pawns after Bxf6 for the bishop pair and open lines.

typical_structures.structure: Dutch Stonewall or Classical with Black's f5/e6/d5 chain; doubled f-pawns after Bxf6 exf6.

character.notes: Dutch positions are unbalanced; here White's e4 break and Black's weak king side make play double-edged, though quieter lines exist. Not sure.

soundness.notes: A sound if unambitious White try; Black has no problems.

structure.notes: Centre undecided: Black chooses Stonewall, Classical or ...d5 structures.

approach.notes: A sideline against the Dutch that strong players use occasionally.

sublines_that_differ.name: 3.Bg5 e6
sublines_that_differ.how: Black avoids doubled pawns; White can follow with Bxf6 and e4.

character.reason: Dutch positions are unbalanced and the e4 break is risky; uncertain.

soundness.reason: A playable White try; Black is fine.

approach.reason: Less common but played by strong players.

plans.reason: Bxf6 exf6 doubles Black's f-pawns in the main line.
